passage: In Class Four, the teacher held up two ribbons and asked which was longer. Tejas could see plainly that the blue one was. But the first child said red, and so did the second, and the third. By the time it was Tejas's turn, his heart thumped. He looked at the ribbons again. Blue was longer; he was sure. "Red," he said, softly. Ankita, sitting near the window, said, "Blue," and the class giggled. Tejas looked at his shoes and wished he had said it too. At fifteen, Tejas sat with a group who agreed that a new film was brilliant. He had thought it was slow and confused. They also agreed that their classmate Hansa was "so annoying." He had actually found her quick and funny. Everyone nodded. "Yeah," said Tejas. "It was great." On the bus home he found himself wondering if he had misjudged the film and whether perhaps Hansa really was irritating. He could not tell if he had changed his mind or had only kept quiet.

qa.q: Which ribbon did Tejas see was longer?
qa.a: He saw that the blue ribbon was longer.

qa.q: How does Tejas's giving in at the ribbons compare with his giving in at fifteen?
qa.a: At the ribbons he said red although he could see blue was longer, and at fifteen he said the film was great and let Hansa be called annoying although he thought otherwise. The first time he knew he was going along, but the second time he began to doubt his own view.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling when he said "Red" after the class had picked red?
qa.a: He felt anxious and afraid of being laughed at, so he gave up what he saw.

qa.q: What could Tejas do next time a whole group agrees on something he doubts?
qa.a: He could look for one friend, like Ankita, who sees it differently, or say quietly that he sees it another way.

grounding: The same person conforms under group agreement at two ages: naming the wrong ribbon in a class, and adopting a group's opinion of a film and a classmate at fifteen.
